power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Colocalization analyses were performed to assess whether gene expression and outcome associations within a locus were consistent with a shared causal variant. Five mutually exclusive hypotheses were evaluated: H0) no association with the exposure or the phenotype; H1) association with the exposure and not the outcome; H2) association with the outcome and not the exposure; H3) association with the outcome and the exposure by independent SNPs; H4) association with the outcome and the exposure by one shared SNP. The posterior probabilities (PP) of H0-H4 sum to 1, with PP of H4 (PPH4) > 0.70 considered evidence supporting colocalization (61). We performed colocalization analyses using coloc.abf() in the R package coloc (version 5.2.3) (58). SMR, SMR-multi, and HEIDI analyses were performed using the SMR software tool (v1.4.2) (54). All other statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.2), and all tests were twotailed. These analyses were performed with the University of Queensland Research Computing Centre's Bunya supercomputer (62). Power calculation. Statistical power was calculated to determine the minimum detectable effect size for each validated topiramate target across all psychiatric outcomes. We used the mRNd tool (63) (https://shiny.cnsgenomics.com/mRnd/) to estimate the minimum detectable effect size at 80% power for each gene expression-outcome pair. Type I error rates (α) were set at 0.05, 0.005 and 0.00125, corresponding to the nominal, primary, and exploratory significance thresholds used in this study.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P>0.05", "p > 0.05"), Sentence = c("Conversely, we found no significant associations between any topiramate proxies and AN, even at the relaxed nominal significance threshold (P>0.05) (Figure 2).", "Furthermore, the association with CA4 expression in the brain did not reach nominal significance (p > 0.05), although the 95% CIs overlapped with those for blood CA4." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.
